vignette:
She is 46, a Middle Eastern woman who has built a steady, competent life as a pharmacist, someone colleagues describe as calm in a crisis and meticulous about details. Before her son's illness, she is the kind of person who keeps moving, who solves problems quickly, who prides herself on being reliable. She lives alone now and speaks of herself as single with a kind of dry practicality, though the larger truth of her life is that for years she has organized everything around being a mother.

The trauma begins when her child becomes suddenly and gravely ill. At first, she assumes it is something routine, the kind of fever or infection that children get and recover from. She knows medicine well enough to notice the seriousness, but not enough to protect herself from the shock of hearing the words "life-threatening." Once the emergency workup starts, time changes shape. She describes the hospital as a place where days blur into one another under fluorescent lights, where she can no longer trust her own sense of what is happening. She remembers trying to stay useful, asking questions, tracking medication names, reading monitors, but inside she feels a rising panic she cannot share with her child. She learns how to smile while her body is trembling.

During those first weeks, she sleeps in fragments, if at all. Every phone ring makes her stomach drop. She begins to scan faces for meaning before anyone speaks. At work, she is physically present but mentally split; she fills prescriptions on autopilot, double-checking everything because mistakes suddenly feel catastrophic. She notices that she cannot tolerate small uncertainties the way she once could. A delayed test result, a missed call, a phrase from a physician that sounds slightly ambiguous-all of it can send her spiraling into worst-case thinking. She keeps picturing the hospital room, the machines, the possibility that she will lose her child. Even now, she says, there are moments when she is sure she can feel again the exact coldness in her hands from that time.

After her child survives the acute medical crisis and returns home, she expects relief to come cleanly, but it does not. Instead, she finds herself living as though the danger is merely hidden. She watches her child constantly, listening for changes in breathing, watching for signs of fatigue or pain, unable to let her guard down. When the child coughs or looks pale, her heart races before she can think. She has trouble being in the present because part of her is always braced for the next emergency. She keeps emergency phone numbers nearby, checks medications repeatedly, and rereads discharge instructions even when she knows them by heart. Her mind returns uninvited to images of the hospital bed and the fear that she was too late, that a tiny delay could have changed everything.

She also becomes more easily startled and more irritable, though she tries to hide it. Noise in the home feels unbearable at times. She can become sharply angry over minor disruptions, then feel guilty for it. She is ashamed that, after surviving something so serious, she does not feel grateful in the simple way others seem to expect. Instead, she feels tense, jumpy, and exhausted. She describes a strange numbness on some days, as if her feelings are muffled behind glass, and then, without warning, grief or fear breaks through so intensely that she has to stop what she is doing. She avoids medical television, certain neighborhoods near the hospital, and conversations that linger on childhood illness. Even in the pharmacy, she sometimes notices a child's cough or a parent's anxious face and feels herself pulled back into that earlier terror.

Over time, her world narrows around safety. She works hard, continues to function, continues to be dependable, but her life is organized by vigilance. She says she has become someone who always anticipates loss. In sessions, she speaks about the period after the illness as a time when her body never fully understood that the emergency had passed. She is aware that others see a competent professional, a mother who managed an impossible situation, but her private experience is of having been permanently altered by those days in the hospital. The fear did not end when her child came home; it followed her, settling into her thoughts, her sleep, and the way she moves through each ordinary day.
